extracted.subtask_description: Practical laboratory procedures and precautions for performing quantitative combustion and oxidation experiments (collection/measurement of water, CO2, O2, gas drying, apparatus design, and safety). Focused on pneumatic-chemical apparatus and measurement techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condense and collect water formed by combustion
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect water formed during combustion by passing the combustion air through a bocal/serpentine so that vapour condenses on cooling surfaces and falls to be weighed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a sequence of condensers (bocal A, serpentin 17 & 18) so that part of the vapor condenses on the bocal walls and the rest in the serpentine as the air cools; remaining dissolved water can be absorbed by a deliquescent salt in a subsequent tube (19 & 20). Weigh the lamp with its reservoir and oil before and after to determine the mass of produced water.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remove and quantify carbonic acid (CO2) with alkalies
rubrics_metrics.description: Absorb CO2 from the combustion gases by passing them through bottles of potash solution (or similar alkali).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use many bottles in series (author used at least nine) filled halfway with potash liqueur, exhausted of CO2 by lime beforehand. Finish with a bottle of limewater as the most sure, sensitive reagent: if it does not cloud, CO2 has been removed to negligible amounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dry gases before final measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove moisture from gases prior to final gasometric measurement using deliquescent/desiccant materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pass the gas through a tube containing deliquescent salt (tube 28 & 29) so as to strip water left after alkali bottles; this prevents water vapor from biasing gas volumes in the gasometer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test residual gas composition by chemical reagent
rubrics_metrics.description: After removal of CO2 and water, sample the residual gas and determine proportions of oxygen and nitrogen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct tests on gas samples (from gasometer) with reagents such as sulfide of potash to determine the proportion of oxygen and nitrogen in the residual gas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for small inevitable losses when assembling apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that small amounts of oil burn and small volumes of air may escape while adjusting or fastening apparatus parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These losses are small in large experiments but must be estimable; include them in the experimental accounting when evaluating results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control wick length externally to maintain correct fuel supply
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide external mechanism to lengthen or shorten the wick without opening the combustion vessel to maintain optimal combustion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a rod (31–34) passing through a leather box actuated by a rack-and-pinion for smooth adjustment; avoid exceeding the proper wick length to prevent capillary overfeeding and soot/fume production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid supplying pure oxygen when burning volatile alcohols in closed vessels
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not perform alcohol (spirit) combustion in oxygen-filled closed vessels because of high detonation risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alcohol vapour can dissolve into contained air and produce an explosive mixture (author reports violent detonation). If oxygen must be used, limit sample size to minute quantities (10–12 grains) and accept large relative errors; safer to use open vessels or dilute conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide safe method for producing ether-air combustible mixtures
rubrics_metrics.description: Generate ether vapour in air by bubbling air through a reservoir so the air dissolves ether progressively and becomes flammable without detonating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct a reservoir with a double bottom and multiple downpipes so gas bubbles through ether (reservoir abcd, pipes ef etc.). Beware of producing an excess of ether in the mixture—this prevents burning in closed vessels and requires additional atmospheric air. Lateral air injection may extinguish the flame if it is too mobile and poorly adherent to the wick; apparatus adjustments are needed to stabilize combustion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dedicated apparatus for hydrogen-oxygen combustion with controlled feeds
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ a vessel (matras/balloon) with separate feed tubes from H2 and O2 gasometers and a vacuum line, with an ignition electrode to ignite the mixing gases safely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare the vessel by evacuating it, then introduce oxygen and measure its amount by the gasometer limb. Introduce hydrogen through a very small opening and ignite via an electric spark between the metal ball L and the orifice d'. Control pressures: hydrogen should enter with 1.5–2 inches water pressure, oxygen with at most 3 lines; these settings balance flame speed. Stop the run when the flame weakens to avoid back-mixing into the oxygen reservoir.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dry gases with alkaline packing (tubes MM, NN)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pass gases through tubes packed with dry alkali (potash, or preferably dry lime salts) to remove water vapour before combustion or measurement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fill tubes with coarse potash concreted and free of CO2; subsequently the author found dry nitrate or muriate of lime in coarse powder removes more water per given quantity of air.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure gas quantities by gasometer limb readings and weight of condensate
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantify amounts of gases introduced or consumed by reading gasometer limb positions and determine formed water by weighing condensate collected in the vessel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note gasometer limbe before and after introduction to compute the volume introduced. Condensed water collects on vessel walls and pools at the bottom; knowing the vessel weight permits accurate determination of water mass. Example result reported: 100 parts by weight of water correspond to 85 oxygen and 15 hydrogen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent backflow and mixing of gases by terminating combustion appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Stop combustion promptly when flame weakens to prevent hydrogen (higher pressure reservoir) from mixing into the oxygen reservoir.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Close the hydrogen feed valve as soon as the flame shows marked weakening to avoid unexpected gas migration into other reservoirs; maintain vigilance throughout runs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeat combustion cycles with evacuation and refilling for successive runs
rubrics_metrics.description: After a combustion run, re-evacuate the vessel and refill oxygen before subsequent burns to maintain controlled amounts and dryness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform vacuuming with the pump via the vacuum line, then fill with oxygen as before; this allows multiple successive measurements from repeated runs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use serpentine condenser with heated chimney for alcohol combustion
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ a serpentine coil in a cooled bath and a double-envelope hot chimney to keep ascending vapours from condensing until they reach the serpentine, ensuring condensate returns through the downward coil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct serpentin EF in a metal bucket ABCD and a double tube chimney GH with ~1-inch sand-filled gap; maintain upper chimney warm to prevent condensation there, and keep serpentine cold (by water) so condensed water descends into the receiving bottle. Under careful operation one may recover about 17 ounces of water from combustion of 16 ounces of alcohol.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perform calcination/oxidation in closed, measured air volumes to observe oxygen uptake
rubrics_metrics.description: Oxidize metals in closed vessels (bell-jar over capsule or sealed cornue) to detect decrease in air volume and relate it to oxygen combination with the metal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods: Priestley-style capsule under a bell jar immersed in water and evacuate to a set level, or seal a cornue after expelling part of its air; heat the metal and observe volume decrease and weight change. These closed conditions reveal true cause of weight increases during calcination. Avoid sealing without first removing air to prevent explosion from thermal expansion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preheat vessels before hermetic sealing to avoid rupture
rubrics_metrics.description: Heat the cornue/vessel before fully sealing so that thermal expansion of trapped air does not cause bursting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warm the vessel and draw off part of the air before final sealing and weigh; failing to remove some internal air before sealing risks explosive failure when heated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize differences in metals' affinities for oxygen
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for the fact that metals oxidize to different extents: gold, silver, and platinum resist oxidation; other metals oxidize variably depending on temperature and oxidant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use blowpipe, airflow, or oxygen to accelerate oxidation for metals with greater affinity; for laboratory demonstrations choose suitable metal forms (fine wires or strips) and use iron/steel shavings or twisted filaments to facilitate ignition and oxidation (procedure attributed to Ingen-Housz).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer methods and reagents for preparing oxygen that maximize purity and economy
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain oxygen from several sources (red oxide of mercury, manganese dioxide with nitrate, heated oxygenated muriate of potash). Choose method balancing purity, cost, and required vessel materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best/purest oxygen: evolved from muriate oxygéné de potasse (oxygenated muriate of potash) by simple heat; reject initial gas portions contaminated with air. Oxygen from mercury oxide or other salts requires porcelain/gritware vessels and may need stronger heat. To remove CO2 from collected oxygen pass gas through a caustic alkaline liquor; nitrogen contamination remains and can be quantified by leaving oxygen in contact with sulfide (sulfure de soude or potasse) for ~15 days to absorb oxygen and leave nitrogen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revive mercury oxide to obtain oxygen and collect mercury condensate
rubrics_metrics.description: Heat oxide of mercury in a cornue fitted with a long glass tube leading under inverted bells in water; collect oxygen and the revived mercury accumulates in a receiving vessel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gas flow begins when the cornue is red-hot. Discard the first portions of gas (air contamination). Collect revived mercury at the tube end in water. Note that oxygen produced often contains ~10% nitrogen and trace CO2 unless purified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale experiments sufficiently to reduce relative measurement error
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer experiments of appreciable size since very small sample masses produce proportionally large measurement errors that undermine confidence in results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small combustions (e.g., 10–12 grains of alcohol) are subject to large relative uncertainties. Where feasible, increase sample size and design apparatus to accommodate larger quantities without compromising safety or accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety precautions regarding explosive mixtures and thermal effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipate detonation risks in closed vessels with flammable vapours and avoid operations where sudden gas release or thermal expansion could cause violent consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: dissolving alcohol in trapped air led to violent explosion of the bell jar. Avoid using oxygen in confined spaces with volatile vapours; if using large-volume vessels (bocal ~1400 cubic inches) be aware that detonation consequences would be severe. Take measures such as limiting sample size, venting before sealing, and having emergency procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider multiple contributing factors in detonation and explosive force
rubrics_metrics.description: When studying powder explosions or detonations, account not only for gas expansion but also the caloric (heat) released, steam formation, and possible water decomposition that can generate hydrogen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effects of powder depend on amount of gas liberated, heat liberated (which increases gas temperature and expansion), decomposition of water yielding hydrogen (very light and highly expanding), and vaporization of un-decomposed water (large volumetric change). Experimental analysis of detonations can reveal constituents of reactive salts (e.g., nitre).
